questions.q: How does a positron compare with an electron?
options: A positron has a larger mass than an electron and a positive charge
A positron has the same mass as an electron but carries a positive charge
A positron has the same charge as an electron but a much smaller mass
A positron is a neutral particle with the same mass as an electron
questions.explanation: Positrons are the opposite of electrons: they have the same mass, but carry a positive charge. The positron is the antiparticle of the electron — same mass, opposite (positive) charge — and when a positron and an electron collide they immediately annihilate each other.

questions.q: In pair production, an incoming gamma ray near a nucleus converts its energy into mass. Why are two particles — an electron and a positron — produced rather than just one?
options: Because momentum must be conserved and a single particle cannot carry it
Because the gamma ray always splits its energy exactly in half
Because charge needs to be conserved, so two particles of opposite sign are produced
Because the nucleus absorbs one of the particles, leaving a pair
questions.explanation: When an incoming gamma ray collides with a nucleus, the energy of the gamma ray is converted into mass (E = mc2), but because charge needs to be conserved, two particles of opposite sign are produced — an electron and a positron. The photon has zero charge, so the negative electron and positive positron together keep the total charge at zero.

questions.q: What is produced when an electron and a positron (or any particle and its antiparticle) collide and annihilate each other?
options: A single gamma ray carrying all the energy
A neutron and a neutrino
Two gamma rays, with total energy equal to 2mec2
A smaller particle plus a gamma ray
questions.explanation: An electron and a positron, or indeed any particle and its antiparticle, can collide and annihilate each other, producing two gamma rays. The energy released equals 2mec2 — the rest mass of both particles converted into electromagnetic energy, shared equally as two gamma photons travelling in opposite directions.

questions.q: In beta-plus (β+) decay a positron is emitted from the nucleus. What happens inside the nucleus, and to the atomic number?
options: A neutron changes into a proton and an electron, so the atomic number rises by one
A proton changes into a neutron and a positron, so the atomic number falls by one
A proton changes into a neutron and a positron, so the atomic number rises by one
An electron is absorbed by a proton, so the atomic number stays the same
questions.explanation: In β+ decay the proton changes into a neutron and a positron; the neutron stays in the nucleus while the positron is emitted. The mass number is unchanged, but because a proton has become a neutron the number of protons — the atomic number — decreases by one. This is the reverse of β− decay, where a neutron transforms into a proton and an electron and the atomic number increases by one.

questions.q: From memory: explain why positron-electron annihilation must produce TWO gamma photons in opposite directions, rather than a single photon.
keyPoints: Just before annihilation the positron and electron are essentially at rest, so the total momentum of the system is very nearly zero.
By conservation of momentum, the total momentum of the products must also be zero.
A single photon always carries momentum and can never have zero momentum, so one photon is forbidden.
Two photons emitted in opposite directions (about 180° apart) carry equal and opposite momenta that cancel to zero, satisfying conservation of momentum.
questions.explanation: The load-bearing word is 'momentum'. If you stated that the pair annihilates at rest (zero momentum), that one photon cannot have zero momentum, and that two opposite photons cancel, grade yourself Good or Easy. If you only said 'two gamma rays come out', that is the what but not the why — grade Again or Hard.

questions.q: An electron (m = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg) and a positron (also m = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg) collide and are annihilated. Calculate the total energy released. Take c = 3.0 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹.
working: All of the rest mass of both particles is converted into energy, so \(E = 2m_e c^2\).
questions.explanation: The electron and positron annihilate, so the energy released equals the rest mass of both particles times the speed of light squared, E = 2mec2 ≈ 1.64 × 10⁻¹³ J. This is shared equally between two gamma photons, so each carries about 8.2 × 10⁻¹⁴ J, which is 0.511 MeV.

questions.q: Calculate the energy released in the beta-plus decay of carbon-11 to boron-11. Atomic masses: C-11 = 11.011 43 u, B-11 = 11.009 31 u, electron/positron = 0.000 55 u each; 1 u ≡ 931.5 MeV.
questions.explanation: Because the quoted masses are atomic masses they include the orbiting electrons, so the electron bookkeeping must be handled before converting the mass loss to energy. Multiply the mass loss in u by 931.5 (and stop — the per-c² is already built into that factor): 0.00102 × 931.5 ≈ 0.950 MeV, carried away as kinetic energy of the positron and neutrino.

questions.q: The electron is one of the six leptons. State its antiparticle and how that antiparticle's charge compares.
keyPoints: Each of the six leptons has an antiparticle.
For the electron, the antiparticle is the positron.
The positron has the same mass as the electron but is positively charged (opposite sign of charge).
Leptons such as the electron are fundamental particles — they have no internal structure.
questions.explanation: From the lepton table: for the electron, the antiparticle is the positron, which is positively charged (like the anti-muon and anti-tau). If you named the positron and noted it has the same mass but opposite, positive charge, grade Good or Easy.

questions.q: A patient is given a fluorine-18 tracer for a PET scan. Explain how the scan produces an image, and justify why a short-lived isotope is used. (6 marks)
questions.modelAnswer: Fluorine-18, carried in FDG (a glucose analogue), is injected and concentrates in metabolically active tissue because the body treats FDG like glucose. Fluorine-18 is a positron emitter: each emitted positron travels a few millimetres, meets a nearby electron, and annihilates, producing two gamma photons of 0.511 MeV travelling in opposite directions (about 180° apart). A ring of detectors around the patient registers the two photons in coincidence — simultaneously, on opposite sides — and the straight line joining those two detectors, the line of response, passes through the annihilation point. A computer combines millions of these lines of response to reconstruct a three-dimensional image of tracer concentration, mapping metabolic activity and revealing features such as tumours or active brain regions. A short-lived isotope is used because the half-life must be long enough to inject the tracer, let it spread and run the scan, but short enough that it clears the body quickly so the radiation dose stays low; fluorine-18's half-life of about 110 minutes threads that needle.

criteria.descriptor: Tracer (FDG) concentrates in metabolically active tissue because it behaves like glucose.
Positron emitted, annihilates with an electron producing two 0.511 MeV gamma photons in opposite directions.
Coincidence detection by a surrounding ring of detectors registers the two simultaneous, opposite photons.
The line of response joining the two detectors passes through the annihilation point.
Millions of lines of response are combined to reconstruct a 3D image of tracer concentration / metabolic activity.
Justifies the half-life: long enough to image but short enough to clear quickly and keep dose low (F-18 ≈ 110 min).

questions.explanation: Use the TRACER hook (Tracer, Reaches tissue, Annihilation, Coincidence, Establish the line, Reconstruct) to hit every step. The discriminating point on half-life is that longer is worse: more dose, slower clearance.

questions.q: How was the positron first discovered, and by whom?
options: Paul Dirac observed it directly in a cloud chamber in 1928
In 1933 Carl Anderson, investigating cosmic ray showers, observed a particle with the same mass as the electron but a positive charge
Enrico Fermi created it by irradiating paraffin with neutrons
It was first produced inside a particle accelerator at CERN
questions.explanation: In 1933 Carl Anderson, investigating the charged particles in cosmic ray showers, observed a particle that had the same mass as the electron but with a positive charge — the positron. His chamber sat in a strong magnetic field so a positively charged particle curved one way and a negatively charged particle the other. (Dirac had predicted antimatter from his equation earlier; Anderson anchored it in the lab.)
